articles.title: Epidemiologia, Vol. 7, Pages 169: Hospital Mortality During and After the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency in Western Mexico: A Retrospective Observational and Time-Series Study
articles.description: Background/Objectives: The COVID-19 pandemic altered hospital mortality patterns and challenged existing surveillance systems. This study characterized mortality during and after the public health emergency at a secondary-care hospital in western Mexico. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, single-center study using descriptive epidemiology and time-series analysis. All-cause mortality was assessed from March 2017 to May 2024, with the pre-pandemic period used to establish reference limits and calibrate Holt–Winters models for pneumonia mortality. Annual COVID-19-specific mortality and hospital case-fatality rates were estimated for 2020–2023. Results: Among 1099 patients admitted with COVID-19, 510 died, resulting in an overall hospital-based case-fatality rate (CFR) of 46.41% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 43.47–49.36). The overall institution-recorded COVID-19 mortality rate per beneficiary population was 21.24 (95% CI: 19.44–23.12) deaths per 100,000 beneficiary-years. Both indicators peaked in 2021, reaching 42.40 (95% CI: 37.33–47.77) deaths per 100,000 beneficiaries and 57.63% (95% CI: 52.96–62.17), respectively. Among deceased patients, 61.18% were men, the median age was 67 (IQR: 57.00–75.00) years, and the most frequent comorbidities were hypertension (58.63%), diabetes mellitus (39.61%), and chronic kidney disease (22.94%). From March 2020 to May 2023, 3190 all-cause deaths were observed compared with 2774.46 expected deaths, corresponding to approximately 416 excess deaths and a cumulative P-score of 14.98% (5.92% in the sensitivity analysis). Pneumonia mortality peaked at 163 deaths in January 2021, followed by four progressively smaller peaks and a subsequent decline to within or below the historical reference range. Conclusions: Institutional mortality peaked in 2021. Combining mortality indicators with time-series analysis may strengthen hospital surveillance during and after public health emergencies.

articles.title: Australia declares substandard housing a public health emergency
articles.description: In Australia, the housing affordability and quality crisis has crossed into public health territory. The Centre for Excellence in Healthy Housing at the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) released the Australian Healthy Housing Handbook, characterizing the current state of the nation's housing stock as a public health emergency. The report indicates that approximately 2.5 million Australian households live in conditions deemed hazardous to their health. These environments are marked by excessive moisture, mold, inadequate ventilation, and a lack of protection against extreme temperatures. Racheal White, the Deputy Minister for Health and Aged Care, presented the document in Canberra, emphasizing a direct link between substandard housing and serious pathological conditions. These include respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, mental health disorders, developmental delays in children, and a reduction in overall life expectancy and labor productivity. The report's authors note that the healthcare system is forced to expend significant resources treating illnesses caused by cold, heat, or mold in residential settings.
